report:
## Conclusion

Yes — strong evidence from multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses shows that offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) in addition to standard testing services substantially increases the number of people who get tested for HIV.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs among key populations (men who have sex with men and transgender people) found HIVST increased uptake of testing by 1.45 times (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.20–1.75) compared with standard testing alone (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/). A related, more comprehensive review pooling 13 RCTs found an even larger effect—HIVST more than doubled testing uptake (RR 2.09, 95% CI 1.69–2.58, p<0.0001), rated as moderate-certainty evidence, with benefits seen across different service-delivery models (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589537021002716). A meta-analysis focused on adults in Africa similarly concluded that HIVST significantly boosted testing uptake, particularly among men and young people who are otherwise hard to reach (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498).

This body of evidence, largely from trials among priority and hard-to-reach populations (MSM, partners of ART clients, pregnant women, emergency department attendees), underpinned the World Health Organization's 2016 recommendation—reaffirmed and strengthened in 2019 and 2023—that HIVST should be offered as part of HIV testing services, based on moderate-quality evidence of increased uptake and frequency of testing (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36).

While linkage to care after a positive self-test result remains a secondary challenge requiring support, the core finding is consistent and robust: offering HIVST as an additional option reliably increases overall HIV testing rates.
